name: RU58841

lead: RU58841 is an experimental non-steroidal topical antiandrogen originally developed by Roussel Uclaf in the 1990s as a hair-loss candidate. Its development stopped, and it never reached approval.

It is sold online as a research chemical and is popular among hair-loss communities as a finasteride alternative. Evidence is limited to animal and early studies, with no established human safety profile.

paras: It binds the androgen receptor and blocks DHT from activating it in scalp follicles, intended to act locally with minimal systemic absorption. Evidence for this comes from animal models such as the stumptail macaque, not from controlled human trials.

Unknown human toxicity, systemic absorption and long-term effects are the main concerns. It is unapproved, sold by unregulated vendors in varying purity, often in alcohol-based solutions that may irritate the scalp. Reports of use come mainly from anecdote rather than clinical data.

lead: RU58841, also known as PSK-3841 or HMR-3841, is a nonsteroidal antiandrogen originally developed by the French company Roussel Uclaf. It was later investigated by ProStrakan (earlier ProSkelia and Strakan) as a topical treatment for androgen-dependent conditions including acne, pattern hair loss and excess hair growth [1]. It is structurally related to nilutamide and other nonsteroidal antiandrogens [1].

It has never been approved as a medicine. Published research consists of cell, rodent, macaque and xenograft studies from the 1990s, and no controlled human trial of its effect on hair is known to the sources reviewed [2][3][4][5].

Users in hair-loss and bodybuilding forums describe it as a topical androgen blocker used as an alternative or add-on to finasteride or dutasteride, typically obtained as a chemical sold outside regulated pharmacy channels [6][7][8][9].

paras: The compound was explored for androgen-dependent skin and hair conditions: androgenetic alopecia, acne and hirsutism [1]. Patent filings from 2000 to 2001 list it among antiandrogens that could be combined with relaxin in hair-growth compositions [10][11]. Forum users describe it as an experimental hair-loss treatment, usually discussed alongside minoxidil and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors [6][8][9].
No studies found in humans for hair loss. The existing research is preclinical and is summarised below as such.

In a 1997 study, balding human scalp grafts on nude mice conditioned with testosterone were treated with 1% RU58841 in ethanol or ethanol alone for six months; the abstract reports that control grafts had 28 active follicles, of which only two (7 percent) began a second hair cycle, while treated grafts bore 29 active follicles [12]. A 1998 study found that topical RU58841 increased hair density, thickness and length in the stumptailed macaque model of androgenetic alopecia, with no systemic effects detected, and that in cell assays its potency as an androgen-receptor antagonist was comparable to hydroxyflutamide [3]. A 1999 co-culture study used RU58841 to abolish testosterone-induced inhibition of keratinocyte growth in macaque dermal papilla cells [4]. In the fuzzy rat, a model for acne, 1% topical RU58841 produced sebaceous gland regression equivalent to castration, greater than finasteride [2]. A 1998 prostate cell-line study reported that, in cells overexpressing an AR coactivator, several antiandrogens including RU58841 could act as agonists, a finding the authors used to motivate better antiandrogen design [13].

RU58841 blocks the androgen receptor rather than lowering androgen production, a distinction made by forum users comparing it with 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors [5][14]. In animals it is metabolised to cyanonilutamide (RU-56279), which has low receptor affinity but notable antiandrogenic activity, and to RU-59416 [1]. The macaque study authors noted that the compound might cause systemic effects after topical use, but reported none in that model [3].

No human safety profile has been published. Animal and cell studies have examined efficacy rather than toxicity in people, and the 1998 authors flagged the theoretical possibility of systemic exposure after topical application [3]. Forum members have described use alongside testosterone replacement or anabolic steroids to manage hair loss [8][15].

Roussel Uclaf developed the compound, and per Wikipedia it was initially developed in the 1980s [1]. Animal hair studies were published in 1997 to 1999 [3][4][12]. A T Nation poster in 2013 described it as abandoned partway through trials; this is a forum characterisation [16]. A 2026 organic chemistry paper used RU58841 as an example of a bioactive alcohol in a synthetic-method study, unrelated to its use on hair [17].

RU58841 is not a marketed drug in any jurisdiction covered by the sources. T Nation users mention that the compound is costly and that some consider the raw powder to save money, and that one must find a vehicle that lets the topical work [6][16]. A 2004 poster asked if others had heard of it [18].

lore.intro: On T Nation and similar forums, RU58841 appears as an option for people managing hair loss on testosterone therapy or steroids, or who want to avoid oral finasteride [8][9][15].
